text: Projects read: Bangladesh Rural Electrification and Renewable Energy Development II (RERED II, P131263; approved 2012, closed December 2023; PAD and ICR) and Nepal Private Sector-Led Mini-Grid Energy Access Project (P149239; approved January 2019, closing September 2026; PAD and the 2025 restructuring paper; no ICR yet).

RERED II - justification: it scaled up IDCOL's solar home system (SHS) program, which was expected to reach about 2 million systems by end-2012, with a target of another 4 million by 2016 (PAD p. 5). Systems are sold on microfinance through partner organizations; a US$20 grant per system is kept only for systems of 30 Wp and below for the poorest households, down from US$90 in 2003 (the life-cycle cost gap with kerosene lanterns) (PAD p. 7). The economic analysis valued avoided kerosene and battery charging: SHS EIRR 43%, FIRR 26% for 550,000 units; solar mini-grids (42 planned) were justified by cost-effectiveness against diesel, with a mini-grid FIRR of 13.7% at a 32 BDT/kWh tariff, on the assumption that sites would be chosen where the grid would not arrive for more than 8 years (PAD pp. 19-20).

RERED II - what proved difficult: the ICR's key assumptions were slow grid expansion, willingness to pay and trusted partner organizations (ICR p. 12). The slow-grid assumption failed: the government's free distribution of SHS and accelerated grid expansion led to early cessation of SHS deployment and solar mini-grid development, and the delivery models for mini-grids, biogas captive plants and solar irrigation pumps were harder than expected (ICR pp. 25-26). Results at closing: 1.20 million SHS (appraisal target 0.55 million, raised to 1.20 million); 1,303 solar irrigation pumps against a target of 1,987; 5.28 million households, farmers and businesses with clean energy against 6.09 million (ICR p. 26). Ex post, mini-grids and bio-electricity had much higher capital costs than assumed, while other activities beat appraisal returns; efficiency was rated Substantial and the outcome Satisfactory (ICR pp. 29-30).

Nepal - justification: the PDO is to increase generation capacity from renewable mini-grids by mobilizing private ESCOs; targets were 3.8 MW, 126,000 people with new or improved service and US$3.36 million of private capital (PAD pp. 13, 30). Financing assumed about 50% capital subsidy for new mini-grids, 20% equity and 30% debt through partner banks (PAD pp. 14, 21). Economic returns were about 25% for hydro and 21% for solar mini-grids (20% and 15% without GHG benefits), valued against diesel generation; financial IRRs were about 15% (hydro), 11% (solar) and 14% (interconnection at 70% utilization), and sensitivity tests said the schemes stay viable with large cost overruns or lower utilization (PAD pp. 21-22).

Nepal - what proved difficult: COVID-19 lockdowns in China delayed equipment; distress in Nepal's banks in 2020-2023 and higher interest rates made the subprojects, especially the two hydropower plants, financially unviable until UK FCDO money was added, so financial close came only in July 2024; and the design relying on private developers raising local commercial debt needed long legal and financial preparation (restructuring pp. 6-7). The 2025 restructuring extended closing by 18 months, cancelled US$1.5 million after dropping the 1 MW Monjo Khola plant, and cut the targets to 1.11 MW and 30,000 people (households 1,500 to 918); none of the capacity or access targets had been reached by March 2025 (restructuring pp. 6, 10, 14-15).

Common thread: both projects assumed off-grid demand would hold (slow grid arrival, willingness to pay) and that private intermediaries could finance and deliver; grid expansion in Bangladesh and the cost of local finance in Nepal undermined those assumptions.
